bibliography.abstract: Ongoing global environmental problems, including climate change and biodiversity loss, have emphasized the need to foster environmental awareness and pro-environmental actions in people. Childhood experiences with nature are believed to influence the formation of such attitudes and behaviours. However, rapid urbanization and lifestyle changes significantly limit children’s exposure to nature in cities, increasingly disconnecting them from nature. It is, therefore, crucial to understand how contact with nature develops among children growing up in urban settings and how this may predispose them to adopt pro-environmental attitudes and behaviours, especially in non-Western contexts. This study involved 81 children aged 8 to 12 years living in four central districts of Beijing, China. Children first participated in interviews to qualitatively investigate their environmental moral reasoning regarding nature and its protection. The same participants then completed a set of quantitative scales measuring their contact with nature, environmental knowledge, attitudes, and pro-environmental behaviours. The results revealed that most children expressed an anthropocentric view of protecting nature, emphasizing its utilitarian value for humans, particularly in relation to the collective interests of humanity. Regression analysis of the scale data revealed that contact with nature had both a direct effect on pro-environmental behaviours and an indirect effect mediated by environmental attitudes. In contrast, environmental knowledge was not found to be statistically significant. These findings highlight the importance of fostering children’s connection to nature in cities and can also inform environmental education and urban design and planning aimed at promoting more pro-environmental attitudes and actions among youth.
bibliography.title: Exploring children’s contact with nature and pro-environmental behaviours in Beijing, China

en.caveats: The study relies on a small sample of 81 children from a single city, which may limit the generalizability of the behavioral and attitudinal findings to other urban contexts.
en.what: This study analyzed the relationship between nature exposure and environmental actions using interviews and quantitative scales with 81 children aged 8 to 12 in four central districts of Beijing. Regression analysis showed that contact with nature directly influences pro-environmental behaviors and also acts indirectly through environmental attitudes, whereas environmental knowledge had no statistically significant effect. Qualitative interviews revealed that most participants hold anthropocentric views on conservation, prioritizing nature's utilitarian value and collective human interests.
en.why: The findings demonstrate that direct physical contact with nature, rather than classroom-based environmental knowledge, is the primary driver of pro-environmental behaviors in urban children. This shifts the focus for urban educators and planners from merely delivering environmental facts to actively designing physical spaces that facilitate direct nature interactions.
